title: Intermolecular Forces and Properties
seo_title: Intermolecular Forces Worksheets: Hydrogen Bonds and Boiling Points (High School Chemistry)
standard_text: Plan and conduct an investigation to gather evidence to compare the structure of substances at the bulk scale to infer the strength of electrical forces between particles.
meta_desc: Free high school chemistry worksheets on intermolecular forces (NGSS HS-PS1-3): London forces, dipole-dipole forces, hydrogen bonds, boiling points, states of matter and types of solids. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Bulk properties such as boiling point show how strongly particles attract.
body_html:
How to think about it

Stronger attractions between particles mean higher boiling points.

  • London dispersion forces (all molecules) < dipole-dipole forces (polar molecules) < hydrogen bonds (H on N, O or F).
  • Among similar molecules, more electrons (larger size) means stronger London forces.
  • Boiling separates molecules; it does not break the covalent bonds inside them.
Example

Higher boiling point: H2O or H2S?

Water has hydrogen bonds

Answer: water

Example

Higher boiling point: Cl2 or Br2?

Both London only

Br2 is larger

Answer: bromine

Common mistakes

  • Thinking boiling breaks the bonds inside molecules.
  • Calling the O–H bond inside water a hydrogen bond.
  • Thinking larger molecules have weaker forces.

faq.q: What are the three main intermolecular forces?
faq.a: London dispersion forces (in all molecules), dipole-dipole forces (in polar molecules) and hydrogen bonds (H bonded to N, O or F).

faq.q: Why does water have a high boiling point for its size?
faq.a: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than the forces between similar small molecules such as H₂S.

faq.q: How can you compare forces in a lab?
faq.a: Measure bulk properties such as boiling point, melting point, evaporation rate or surface tension.
